name: Dark Payne's Grey
lede: Dark Payne's Grey darkens [[payne-s-grey]], the blue-grey artists' mixing color, and Ridgway charted this darker tone on plate XLIX of his 1912 color atlas without it later being picked up by the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary.

sections.title: A darkened mixing grey
sections.body:
The name applies dark to [[payne-s-grey]], a blue-grey long used by painters to mix shadows and skies without resorting to black [1]. Ridgway recorded this darker variant in *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912), plate XLIX, hue 49′′′′, tone k [1]. Our library finds no corresponding entry for it in the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary, unlike several of its Ridgway-plate neighbors [1].

Measured against our Color Graph, its closest match is [[arona]], only 2.6 units away and a touch bluer; [[dusky-slate-blue]], [[dark-blue-slate]] and [[dark-violet-slate]] all sit within about 3.3 units, almost the same color on screen [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A match for this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 350 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.5 per cent, as photographed [3]. It is strongest in Post-Impressionist works, 7 of 45 paintings, 10.6 times the archive's overall rate [3]. The earliest dated match is a 1270 panel, *The Mourning Saint John the Evangelist*, a floor on the color's age in painting rather than a claim of its first appearance [3]. As photographed: these are computed color matches on museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test [3].
